say.text: A 45-year-old man with years of dyspepsia gets sudden, severe epigastric pain. Think perforation.
Which site is the **commonest** place for this perforation to occur?

choices.label: Anterior wall, first part of duodenum
Posterior wall, first part of duodenum
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The **anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum** is the commonest perforation site.
The posterior wall is where ulcers bleed, because they erode the gastroduodenal artery.
Think about what lies behind each wall. One wall faces the open peritoneal cavity once it gives way.
The other wall sits against a major artery. Which wall lets gas and stomach contents into the belly?
Not right. The posterior wall feels like the dangerous side, because the gastroduodenal artery lies behind it.
That artery erodes in a posterior ulcer, so the result is bleeding. The commonest perforation site is the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what lies behind each wall: the artery on one side, the open cavity on the other.

say.text: Not right. The lesser curvature feels right, because it is a familiar stomach site and gastric ulcers can perforate.
But the commonest perforation site is the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Duodenal ulcers are the commonest source of perforation, so check the duodenum first.

say.text: An erect chest X-ray shows gas under the diaphragm. Gas that escapes through a perforation rises to lie there.
Which statement about this free gas is right?

choices.label: A perforated peptic ulcer is the most common cause of free gas
Free gas always means a perforated peptic ulcer, so theatre
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Perforated peptic ulcer is the most common cause of pneumoperitoneum, which is a frequency statement.
Other causes exist, so the film has to be read with the clinical picture.
Look at how often the statement says the ulcer causes free gas. Does it say the ulcer is the only cause?
Not right. The ulcer is a classic cause, and the one you must act on fast, so 'always' feels safe.
But perforated peptic ulcer is the most common cause of pneumoperitoneum, not the only one.

sure_note.text: You were sure that free gas means ulcer. Check the phrase 'most common' in the statement.

say.text: A 60-year-old man had a laparoscopy two days ago. His erect film shows free gas under the right diaphragm.
Which reading fits best?

choices.label: Possible residual gas, so read it with the history
Perforated peptic ulcer, so take him to theatre now
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Free gas has other causes, and a recent procedure is one of them, so the history changes the reading.
The ulcer is still the most common cause, so the film alone does not decide the management.
Ask what the recent history can explain before you reach for the most common cause.
Not right. The ulcer is the most common cause of free gas, so 'gas means ulcer' is tempting.
But 'most common' is not 'always', and a recent procedure is a known other cause. Read the gas with the history before you act on the film.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Free gas after a recent procedure should send you back to the history before theatre.
